on the main diagonal only, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the *almost* zero ${\color{blue}{n}}\times {\color{red}{m}}$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma_1^{-1}}, \, {\sigma_2^{-1}}, \, \ldots, \, {\sigma_r^{-1}}
$$

on the main diagonal only.

![](images/d6/d6d6a167747f99c5a48be59ae3e11ca7b5a9188e80ddeb63b8c0f193d991b18c.svg)

we calculate its pseudoinverse as follows:

- **Step 1:** Replace the non-zero elements on the main diagonal with their multiplicative inverses.

- **Step 2:** Transpose the resulting matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {4}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1/3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Therefore, we have

Over Circles and Ellipses"}] :question/problem "Evaluate $\displaystyle \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = y\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction." :question/worked-solution "The notation $\displaystyle\oint$ is used to remind us that we're dealing with a line integral over a *closed* curve.

We will use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
y = \sin{t}.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t)+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180015 :question/id #uuid "2a8909b1-1a48-5c56-ac06-8b954196fc3e" :question/math-academy-id "q-124936"} {:db/id 17592186180172 :question/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "![](images/48/4807f92defb4202359a32ca046073cd138db396a0975164e42b96126ac0cc591.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,1)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186259784 :question/id #uuid "c359f485-3a3d-5def-a8c7-a71d4c1cd8eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-125170" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179735 :knowledge-point/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "![](images/00/00ff3216e6876673a388eb3eaa0e7d02e268f5e679593ebd9fe01e2840099e1b.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+xy\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,2)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+xy\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186259787 :question/id #uuid "6685801b-d2c3-50ec-b8be-f01b7aa1bedc" :question/math-academy-id "q-125238"} {:db/id 17592186326764 :question/id #uuid "d4c5cd42-1163-5d1e-b9ef-190caf4e41ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-39427" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179735 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5d7c30c2-5d42-5648-ae49-5a0c7ec43233" :knowledge-point/title "Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24c7893f-0b53-5740-8fbd-ebe54258cfa1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186324273} {:answer/id #uuid "5f8031ce-b980-5eb0-9766-6549305fa866" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1-\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186324768} {:answer/id #uuid "95bc9fcf-3ac1-5ef9-8027-af87ed0205b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}-\pi \sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186325248} {:answer/id #uuid "b23599ac-9233-5e96-a595-f5c52a1d949f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186325498} {:answer/id #uuid "f81eed55-5dd8-5481-8cb2-750b01e06593" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186326156}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "b23599ac-9233-5e96-a595-f5c52a1d949f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186325498} :answer-field/id #uuid "df8011e5-0bf7-5c27-90ed-97013e5119ed" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186326629}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/c5/c5e026312ab8a2ccfc61a37246c954b56550316661f158743cc2c46411a97f53.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(y-x)\,i-x\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=2$  traversed counterclockwise from the point $(\sqrt{2},0)$ to the point $(0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)\,i-x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\sqrt{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}t]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345267 :question/id #uuid "f314aa29-173f-5141-b324-f3ce0549aed3" :question/math-academy-id "q-77008"} {:db/id 17592186345268 :question/id #uuid Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=3y\,i+2x\,j$ and $C$ is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively, traversed anticlockwise from $A(0,3)$ to $B(-1,0)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively. It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =3y\,i+2x\,j \\  & =9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186414917 :question/id #uuid "019e6ad0-f5c1-533f-a132-64a664a1964d" :question/math-academy-id "q-125235"} {:db/id 17592186414918 :question/id #uuid $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-3,0).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+27{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{[{sin}^{3}⁡t-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{2}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =9[0-(1-\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186414926 :question/id #uuid "d9322f25-3d78-5fb4-87e7-1e944f82fbf4" :question/math-academy-id "q-76984"} {:db/id 17592186179736 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = y\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is the curve $y^3 = x-5$ traversed from the point $A(5,0)$ to the point $B(6,1).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
y^3 = x-5
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
x = y^3 + 5.
$$

So, we can parametrize the curve using

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =({t}^{3}+5)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t^3+5, \qquad
y = t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j \\  & =t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+5)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =t\cdot 3{t}^{2}+({t}^{3}+5)\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{3}+{t}^{3}+5 \\  & =4{t}^{3}+5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{3}+5\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{4}+5t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1+5-0 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180012 :question/id #uuid "d4e0663c-1824-56f9-b923-60eb7cd3a338" :question/math-academy-id "q-124703" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179736 :knowledge-point/id #uuid *Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=t\,i+(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,1\le t\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=2{t}^{2}-1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-1)j \\  & =i+4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j)\cdot (i+4t\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\cdot 4t \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180016 :question/id #uuid "9565c624-6479-5e2a-bbcb-90464f68b7c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-125039"} {:db/id 17592186259719 :question/id #uuid the curve ${y}^{3}=x+3$ traversed from the point $A(-3,0)$ to the point $B(5,2).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
{y}^{3}=x+3\,⟹\,x={y}^{3}-3.
$$

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =({t}^{3}-3)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{3}-3,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =({t}^{3}-3)\,i+{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(({t}^{3}-3))i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =3{t}^{2}i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{3}-3)\,i+{t}^{2}\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =({t}^{3}-3)\cdot 3{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{5}-9{t}^{2}+{t}^{2} \\  & =3{t}^{5}-8{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{t}^{5}-8{t}^{2})\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{6}}{2}-\frac{8{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{{2}^{6}}{2}-\frac{8(2)^{3}}{3})-0 \\  & =32-\frac{64}{3} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Since $y$ is the subject of the equation, a parametrization is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=3{t}^{2}+1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+1)j \\  & =i+6t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j)\cdot (i+6t\,j) \\  & =t\cdot 1+(3{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 6t \\  & =t+18{t}^{3}+6t \\  & =7t+18{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7t+18{t}^{3})\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{7{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{9{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{7(1)^{2}}{2}+\frac{9(1)^{4}}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{16}{2} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186259770 :question/id #uuid "0a252593-58a1-58ca-bfe1-af494ec001df" :question/math-academy-id "q-125049"} {:db/id 17592186259773 :question/id #uuid $F(x,y)=x\,i+2y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡y-x=0$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,e).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡y-x=0\,⟹\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡y.
$$

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+t\,j,\,1\le t\le e.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+2y\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+2t\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+2t\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t}+2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{e}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t}+2t)\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡t}{2}+{t}^{2}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =(\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡e}{2}+{e}^{2})-(0+1) \\  & ={e}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186259774 :question/id #uuid "72883a67-9d43-5b52-b813-4e7994e51be8" :question/math-academy-id "q-125066"} {:db/id 17592186259781 :question/id #uuid :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=2y\,i+{x}^{2}\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $\sqrt{y}=x+3$ traversed from the point $A(-3,0)$ to the point $B(-1,4)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(\sqrt{t}-3)\,i+t\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(\sqrt{t}-3)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{t}-3,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2t\,i+(\sqrt{t}-3)^{2}\,j \\  & =2t\,i+(t-6\sqrt{t}+9)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}-3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2t\,i+(t-6\sqrt{t}+9)\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,i+j) \\  & =2t\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+t-6\sqrt{t}+9 \\  & =\sqrt{t}+t-6\sqrt{t}+9 \\  & =t-5\sqrt{t}+9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(t-5\sqrt{t}+9)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186414923 :question/id #uuid "7481ae6d-9732-54c0-9a0f-c47726a9f80a" :question/math-academy-id "q-125143"} {:db/id 17592186414924 :question/id #uuid :question/problem "Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) =(1-y)^2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(0, 2)$ to the point $B(1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{i}.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =2j+t[i-2j] \\  & =t\,i+(2-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t = 1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
	y = 2-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(1-y)^{2}\,i+x\,j \\  & =(1-(2-2t))^{2}\,i+t\,j \\  & =(2t-1)^{2}\,i+t\,j \\  & =(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-2t)j \\  & =i-2j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i-2j) \\  & =(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\cdot (1)+(t)\cdot (-2) \\  & =4{t}^{2}-6t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}-6t+1\,dt \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}-3+1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180010 :question/id #uuid "88b31475-15e6-5485-a3fc-dfd5113d0f64" :question/math-academy-id "q-124701" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179737 :knowledge-point/id #uuid *Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(3-2t)\,i+(2+3t)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=3\,i+2\,j$ and $b=i+5\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(3\,i+2\,j)+t[(i+5\,j)-(3\,i+2\,j)] \\  & =(3\,i+2\,j)+t(-2\,i+3\,j) \\  & =(3-2t)\,i+(2+3t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3-2t,\,y=2+3t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j \\  & ={e}^{3-2t}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+3t)j \\  & =-2\,i+3\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{3-2t}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,j)\cdot (-2\,i+3\,j) \\  & ={e}^{3-2t}\cdot (-2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =-2{e}^{3-2t}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2{e}^{3-2t}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180011 :question/id #uuid "f0f71dad-242f-524e-855f-4cf34a64efd5" :question/math-academy-id "q-124702"} {:db/id 17592186259768 :question/id #uuid *Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(1+3t)\,i+(1+2t)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=i+j$ and $b=4\,i+3\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(i+j)+t[(4\,i+3\,j)-(i+j)] \\  & =(i+j)+t(3i+2\,j) \\  & =(1+3t)\,i+(1+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=1+3t,\,y=1+2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,i+\sqrt{xy}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+3t+1+2t)\,i+\sqrt{(1+3t)(1+2t)}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\,i+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)j \\  & =3\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\,i+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (3\,i+2\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\cdot 3+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\cdot 2 \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)+2\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)+2\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186259769 :question/id #uuid "73756350-0217-5bec-bce7-083a72fddb57" :question/math-academy-id "q-125048" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179737 :knowledge-point/id #uuid *Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(2+3t)\,i+(3+t)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=2\,i+3\,j$ and $b=5\,i+4\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i+3\,j)+t[(5\,i+4\,j)-(2\,i+3\,j)] \\  & =(2\,i+3\,j)+t(3\,i+j) \\  & =(2+3t)\,i+(3+t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2+3t,\,y=3+t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2{x}^{7}\,i+{5}^{x+y}\,j \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{2+3t+3+t}\,j \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{5+4t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3+t)j \\  & =3\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{5+4t}\,j)\cdot (3\,i+j) \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\cdot 3+{5}^{5+4t}\cdot 1 \\  & =6(2+3t)^{7}+{5}^{5+4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6(2+3t)^{7}+{5}^{5+4t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186259771 :question/id #uuid "5c3d9ed1-0933-5888-a255-a50d1ec9f17c" :question/math-academy-id "q-125052"} {:db/id 17592186259772 :question/id #uuid $$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=2\,i$ and $b=4\,i+2\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i)+t[(4\,i+2\,j)-(2\,i)] \\  & =(2\,i)+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(2t+2)\,i+2t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2t+2\,y=2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j \\  & ={e}^{2t}\,i+{e}^{2t+2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)j \\  & =2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{2t}\,i+{e}^{2t+2}\,j)\cdot (2\,i+2\,j) \\  & ={e}^{2t}\cdot 2+{e}^{2t+2}\cdot 2 \\  & =2{e}^{2t}(1+{e}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{e}^{2t}(1+{e}^{2})\,dt \\  & =(1+{e}^{2}){e}^{2t}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+{e}^{2})({e}^{2}-1) \\  & ={e}^{4}-1\end{aligned}

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-2\,i+j$ and $b=i-j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t[(i-j)-(-2\,i+j)] \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t(3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-2+3t,\,y=1-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)^{2}\,i+{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & =(-2+3t+1-2t)^{2}\,i+{e}^{-2+3t-(1-2t)}\,j \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)j \\  & =3\,i-2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-2}\,j)\cdot (3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\cdot 3+{e}^{5t-3}\cdot (-2) \\  & =3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:tutorial/content "The line integral of a vector-valued function $\mathbf F$ along a piecewise smooth curve $C$ is denoted

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r .
$$

This integral represents the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle from an initial point $A$ to a terminal point $B$ along the curve.

If the curve can be parameterized by the function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ then we can calculate the line integral using the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r= \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,\textrm dt
$$

Often, the trickiest part is finding a parameterization for $C.$ In this lesson, we'll consider several different cases" :tutorial/id #uuid "ec010a30-571c-5ad5-b30a-c18ffdd997e1" $$
y=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}.
$$

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3}{2}){x}^{(-\frac{3}{2}-1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-5/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186244047 :question/id #uuid "d8b68054-81de-5c7a-845b-113fa9329a52" :question/math-academy-id "q-10735"} {:db/id 17592186518174 :question/id #uuid "8ce73f5e-c8df-5814-9aaf-e78dee12c64a" :question/math-academy-id "q-10741" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4d7cab94-65b2-5228-8549-f3ba7717c36b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{11}x" :db/id 17592186517638} {:answer/id #uuid "608c8c54-3777-5d49-8def-13401921a806" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}{x}^{8}" :db/id 17592186517665} {:answer/id #uuid "ad22bea0-0514-5968-a849-0f45c5a43d08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9{x}^{9}" :db/id 17592186517812} {:answer/id #uuid "d7ba16ff-9f57-54e5-b32e-9e736a76872d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{99}{{x}^{10}}" :db/id 17592186517898} {:answer/id #uuid "e52d4e72-b1f6-5c83-8f92-b5cb335afcc1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{99}{{x}^{11}}" :db/id 17592186517922}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186517898} :answer-field/id #uuid "d47a598d-d2c7-5bab-9e38-017b0c639aa7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186518073}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "If $y=\frac{11}{{x}^{9}},$ find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$" :question/worked-solution "We first rewrite the function as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(k f(x)\right) = k \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(f(x)\right)
$$

For example, to differentiate $y=6x^2$, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{d}{dx}(6x^{2}) \\
&= 6 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}) \\
&= 6 \cdot 2x \\
&= 12x
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "882aa12a-1be9-5fa0-8b2f-2a42007270f7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 345 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "774ab8dd-74f7-5649-bbaf-2c137913eac6" :step/math-academy-id two functions, we can take the sum of their respective derivatives:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(u(x) + v(x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} + \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x}
$$

The sum rule also applies to differences:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(u(x) - v(x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} - \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x}
$$

As an example, let's calculate the derivative of the function

$$
y = x^2 + x
$$

We can apply the sum rule to find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2} + x) \\
&= \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}) + \frac{d}{dx}(x) \\
&= 2x + 1
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f81bca0f-c3d3-5653-b4d5-17a0d2af8863" :tutorial/math-academy-id 348 :tutorial/title "The Sum Rule for Differentiation"} :step/id #uuid "51156115-46da-5b79-ab31-debdece8bd51" $$
y=\frac{11}{{x}^{9}}=11{x}^{-9}.

bisector of the segment joining the two points.

For example, suppose that the line $l$ reflects the point $A$ onto $A'$ below. How can we find the equation of $l$?

![](images/79/79ddc15badc704a9c9860207a5156c3a0505ab626572581bcf3146976338a015.png)

The line $l$ is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment $\overline{AA'}$. So, the line of reflection is $y=-1$.

![](images/aa/aa240e562acf388bdf05751e680e917bc8465bad34300334f6b423df46a7d1f3.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "8464dac5-c554-50b1-94c2-4e8df122e9fb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2363 :tutorial/title "Identifying the Line of Reflection"} :step/id #uuid "0b163811-1b76-5f40-981e-e52237413897" :step/math-academy-id 10216 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173106}} {:db/id 17592186173104 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173142 :tutorial/content "We can reflect an object in any line. Consider the diagram below. The two polygons are the mirror images of each other in the line $l$.

![](images/1e/1e4dfb2939916df5d5018320819f14fcec261a1e77c171b551e9868a8c3bebc8.png)

If we want to reflect the quadrilateral $ABCD$ below in the line $l$, we can reflect each vertex separately and then draw the segments between the resulting corresponding vertices.

![](images/a4/a47c41b41ecae2bc4c281e1b90c843ae68fa907a0d2ff49c48454fd80e2977c7.png)

Let's start by reflecting the point $A$. To do this, we need to plot a new point $A'$ on the opposite side of $l$ at an equal distance away from $l$ as the original point $A$.

The original point $A$ is $4$ units to the left of $l$, so we need to plot the new point $A'$ at a distance of $4$ units to the right of $l$.

![](images/33/33bb82c9d0f20df13f46060b9aec21e8c4d1231766926c47b7718bf58e1c5e32.png)

Now let's reflect other vertices of the quadrilateral in the same way:

![](images/00/00ec763ccce462effa024486a6ff09a98b549c61179de18bb850470e835a7627.png)

Finally, we draw segments between the reflected vertices.

17592186050157 :topic/id #uuid "32ad96da-6870-504d-ad58-7d14df8bea1a" :topic/math-academy-id 668} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186079356 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079727 :tutorial/content "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is given by

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d,
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term and $d$ is a common difference.

To illustrate how this works, suppose we want to find the $20$th term of the following arithmetic sequence:

$$
{\color{blue}2}, \: 5, \: 8, \: 11, \: 14, \: \ldots
$$

The first term is $a_1={\color{blue}2},$ and the common difference is 

$$
d=5-2={\color{red}3}.
$$

So, we can write the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =2+(n-1)(3) \\  & =2+3n-3 \\  & =3n-1\end{aligned}
$$

To find the $20$th term, we can use this formula with $n=20\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =3n-1 \\ {a}_{20} & =3(20)-1 \\  & =60-1 \\  & =59\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $20$th term is $a_{20}=59.$ Using the formula was much quicker than writing out all $20$ terms of the sequence!" :tutorial/id #uuid "8a96e03d-29c4-5df5-9a65-7ba58b42a896" The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x = 2pt, \qquad y = pt^2,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(4,8),$ we can substitute $x=4$ and $y=8$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4 &=2pt \\ 8 &=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =p{(\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ 8 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ 8 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x = 2\left(\dfrac 12 \right)t, \qquad y = \left(\dfrac 12 \right)t^2 ,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x = t, \qquad y = \dfrac 12 t^2 .
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048293} {:db/id 17592186048366} {:db/id 17592186048826} {:db/id 17592186088430 :question/id #uuid "bfc19725-defa-5a63-87f9-f8a8fdd626b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-84108"} The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=2pt,\,y=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(1,2),$ we can substitute $x=1$ and $y=2$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}1 &=2pt \\ 2 &=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =2pt \\ \frac{1}{2} & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{2p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =p{(\frac{1}{2p})}^{2} \\ 2 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{4{p}^{2}} \\ 2 & =\frac{1}{4p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=2(\frac{1}{8})t,\,y=(\frac{1}{8}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(0,0),$ and passes through the point $(6,3).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=2pt,\,y=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(6,3),$ we can substitute $x=6$ and $y=3$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6 &=2pt \\ 3 &=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =2pt \\ 3 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{3}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =p{(\frac{3}{p})}^{2} \\ 3 & =p\cdot \frac{9}{{p}^{2}} \\ 3 & =\frac{9}{p} \\ p & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=2(3)t,\,y=(3){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=6t,\,y=3{t}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186087801 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186087629 :question/id #uuid "29cfe1ff-ca64-51f9-8da1-5d0f798711f2" :question/math-academy-id "e-7437"} :knowledge-point/id \begin{aligned}-4 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & =p{(-\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ -5 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ p & =-\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=(-\frac{4}{5}){t}^{2},\,y=2(-\frac{4}{5})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=-\frac{4}{5}{t}^{2},\,y=-\frac{8}{5}t.

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

{:db/id 17592186088697}} {:db/id 17592186088695 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088970 :tutorial/content "The standard parametric equations of a *vertical* parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x = 2pt, \qquad y = pt^2, \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty),
$$

where $p$ is constant.

As usual, the sign of $p$ determines whether the parabola is upward-opening or downward-opening.

- When $p > 0,$ the parabola is upward-opening.

![](images/39/3962fbc2a0fff44300677c89e867c57582473a8e56aedfe0fcf1d20fb9a322c9.png)

- When $p < 0,$ the parabola is downward-opening.

![](images/63/63acc881f875fbf96fb6ef8a8db9fb778669eabbc171e3800e521a48c130aa89.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "a0b858e3-ea45-5f93-903c-65d346ab9b0a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4624 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "283e44b0-129c-5ed3-8eda-f67b74ce0e0d" :step/math-academy-id 28491 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088687}} {:db/id 17592186088696 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088971 :tutorial/content "The parametric equations of a *horizontal* parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x = pt^2, \qquad y = 2pt, \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty),
$$

where $p$ is constant.

This time, the sign of $p$ determines whether the parabola is left-opening or right-opening.

- When $p > 0,$ the parabola is right-opening.

![](images/77/7758fc4d8eaec780a92c548393b48eb1457d6961fb33aa7e4e4e776e71a4fd7a.png)

- When $p < 0,$ the parabola is left-opening.

![](images/28/28f17924216890db2b0f9a6baf914502184ce21d7f5723a933c955e789b1bb23.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "6480b59c-8f91-5c94-8eb9-0f1bfe519e81" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4625 :tutorial/title "The Parametric Equations of Horizontal Parabolas Whose Vertex Is at the Origin"} :step/id #uuid "3c903871-8fc1-5bba-b0a9-757980a0ad09" :step/math-academy-id 28492 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088688}} {:db/id 17592186088697 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088972 :tutorial/content "We've been told that the parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x = 2pt, \qquad y = pt^2, \qquad t\in(-\infty,\infty).
$$

But how do we know that these parametric equations describe a parabola?

First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2pt & ⟹ &  & t & =\frac{x}{2p} \\ y & =p{t}^{2} & ⟹ &  & {t}^{2} & =\frac{y}{p}\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first equation above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{x}{2p})}^{2} \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4{p}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the above into the second equation $t^2 = \dfrac{y}{p},$ we can eliminate the parameter $t$ and rearrange to find the Cartesian equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =\frac{y}{p} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4{p}^{2}} & =\frac{y}{p} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{y}{p}\cdot 4{p}^{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =4py\end{aligned}
$$

This is the Cartesian equation of a vertical parabola, which confirms that the parametric equations describe a vertical parabola.

If we followed the same procedure for the parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0),$ we would obtain that the Cartesian equation of the parabola is $y^2 = 4px.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "eeb3b2df-57fd-5962-bc60-e1e64961038e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4626 :tutorial/title "How Do We Know That the Parametric Equations Describe a Parabola?"} :step/id #uuid "f517edbc-d6fc-5d91-ab9f-1f40acb5734e" :step/math-academy-id 28495}] :activity/title "Parametric Equations of Parabolas" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186087940} {:db/id 17592186088695 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088970 :tutorial/content "The standard parametric equations of a *vertical* parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

where $p$ is constant.

As usual, the sign of $p$ determines whether the parabola is upward-opening or downward-opening.

- When $p > 0,$ the parabola is upward-opening.

![](images/28/28f17924216890db2b0f9a6baf914502184ce21d7f5723a933c955e789b1bb23.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "6480b59c-8f91-5c94-8eb9-0f1bfe519e81" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4625 :tutorial/title "The Parametric Equations of Horizontal Parabolas Whose Vertex Is at the Origin"} {:db/id 17592186088972 :tutorial/content "We've been told that the parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x = 2pt, \qquad y = pt^2, \qquad t\in(-\infty,\infty).
$$

But how do we know that these parametric equations describe a parabola?

First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2pt & ⟹ &  & t & =\frac{x}{2p} \\ y & =p{t}^{2} & ⟹ &  & {t}^{2} & =\frac{y}{p}\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first equation above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{x}{2p})}^{2} \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4{p}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the above into the second equation $t^2 = \dfrac{y}{p},$ we can eliminate the parameter $t$ and rearrange to find the Cartesian equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =\frac{y}{p} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4{p}^{2}} & =\frac{y}{p} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{y}{p}\cdot 4{p}^{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =4py\end{aligned}
$$

This is the Cartesian equation of a vertical parabola, which confirms that the parametric equations describe a vertical parabola.

If we followed the same procedure for the parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0),$ we would obtain that the Cartesian equation of the parabola is $y^2 = 4px.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "eeb3b2df-57fd-5962-bc60-e1e64961038e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4626 :tutorial/title "How Do We Know That the Parametric Equations Describe a Parabola?"} {:db/id 17592186428619 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals Over Parametric Curves"}] :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)=xy^2+ 2xz.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $\mathbf r(t)= \langle e^{t}, t, e^{-t}\rangle$ for $t\in \left[0,1\right],$ evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{C} \nabla f\cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,0,1⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨e,1,\frac{1}{e}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,0,1)$ and $\left(e, 1, \dfrac{1}{e}\right).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(e,1,\frac{1}{e})-f(1,0,1) \\  & =(e(1)^{2}+2\cdot e\cdot \frac{1}{e})-(1(0)^{2}+2(1)(1)) \\  & =(e+2)-2 \\  & =e.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134059 :question/id #uuid "63f96647-0e17-5269-a429-2d3bdcfb1cff" :question/math-academy-id "q-104616" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00980506-979a-5a3c-bb6b-3b50f009bfac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186415067} {:answer/id #uuid "1aeef040-2421-5b1c-b55a-b92ee77dadcc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186415070} {:answer/id #uuid "5daedb86-7dd6-576d-aff0-8f7b1f0062ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "28" :db/id 17592186415078} {:answer/id #uuid "a2214f1f-3631-5be2-85e4-d5102a1c44c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186415083} {:answer/id #uuid "d6de32bd-280a-5c5a-aa34-19f1b3faadf0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186415092}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415078} :answer-field/id #uuid "8d412271-dad8-50a6-a5b4-2d3051bb421a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415100}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+y.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨3t,{t}^{3}⟩$ for $t\in [0,1],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨3,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(3,1).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(3,1)-f(0,0) \\  & =({3}^{3}+1)-({0}^{3}+0) \\  & =(27+1)-0 \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134567 :question/id #uuid "5f3deee5-4f24-50ef-afc8-99c0e1eb0804" :question/math-academy-id "q-99008"} {:db/id 17592186240906 :question/id #uuid "1eb7495c-4bb1-5f06-bc1d-e458481de613" :question/math-academy-id "q-104623" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a528a36-e97e-5732-8fae-1697a81d8ff0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\pi }^{2}+2\pi " :db/id 17592186238153} {:answer/id #uuid "44bbd131-4ecd-540b-ad14-259cefa4dcf3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\pi }^{2}-1" :db/id 17592186238651} {:answer/id #uuid "4ab4b784-0b5f-5e1b-9fde-ec17a7e2873d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi +2" :db/id 17592186238701} {:answer/id #uuid "89f290a7-499e-5b23-8f65-ac96513f25dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186239255} {:answer/id #uuid "ecb83a5e-cf58-56d7-bc9a-928b68a83802" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\pi }^{2}-4\pi " :db/id 17592186240135}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186240135} :answer-field/id #uuid "fbad1630-befd-5b0d-9389-d98b46343814" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240770}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y-{y}^{2}x.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\pi ],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that

$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate $\displaystyle{\int _C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r}$ for $\mathbf F = ye^{xy}\,\mathbf i + xe^{xy}\,\mathbf j.$ 

*Hint: You may wish to use the fact that $\mathbf F$ is conservative.*" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

 

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ such that $\mathbf F = \nabla f.$ Since we're given that $\mathbf F$ is conservative, we know that such a function exists. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =y{e}^{xy}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =x{e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)= e^{xy}.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $\nabla f = \mathbf F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,1⟩, \\ r(1) & =⟨1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,1)$ and $(1,0).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(1,0)-f(0,1) \\  & ={e}^{1\cdot 0}-{e}^{0\cdot 1} \\  & =1-1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186530780} {:db/id 17592186134213 :question/id #uuid "73c892c9-a1e1-5820-84c2-50c996c14b02" :question/math-academy-id "q-39349"} {:db/id 17592186134566 :question/id #uuid "ff7ad628-63c0-5640-b2d2-82a36608b04e" :question/math-academy-id "q-98995" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133879 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e8a1d966-b4a8-5af8-8b10-063cacea6526" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals When the Potential Function Is Not Given"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "21bae757-f490-594c-be1d-7a2d2c77f021" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186360982} {:answer/id #uuid "2d6c9f0e-8b69-578c-b5ae-a56b0b59e2e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186361041} {:answer/id #uuid "356d8fc5-06cd-5609-b39b-96eddcad3b4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186361072} {:answer/id #uuid "be29d524-2692-5e36-bb76-b3ac0de7b124" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186361688} {:answer/id #uuid "ea0cfc9c-4409-56c9-956d-a96016bee45d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186361880}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ea0cfc9c-4409-56c9-956d-a96016bee45d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186361880} :answer-field/id #uuid "f8db0f63-bf1b-537c-b12e-a90d68712f38" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186362205}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the curve $C,$ defined parametrically as

2110} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134760 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135084 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b].$ The fundamental theorem of calculus states that

$$
\int_a^b f'(x)\,\textrm d x = f(b) - f(a).
$$

A similar result, known as **the fundamental theorem for line integrals,** exists for line integrals of conservative vector fields. This theorem can be stated as follows:

*Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ Then,*

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

 

We'll discuss how this theorem is proved in simple cases at the end of the lesson. But for now, let's take a look at a concrete example of how to apply this theorem." :tutorial/id #uuid "0c3e4762-a85a-5881-81ad-857e0bec5a48" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4306 :tutorial/title #uuid "879e7253-5b1c-559d-8414-14057286be07" :step/math-academy-id 35588 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134825}} {:db/id 17592186134860 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135127 :tutorial/content "Let's apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals to evaluate

$$
\int_C \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},
$$

where $f(x,y) = x^2y^3$ and $C$ is the path along the curve $y=x^2$ for $x \in [0,2].$ 

First, we must parameterize the curve $C.$ A suitable parametrization is 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t, \: t^2\right\rangle, \qquad t \in [0,2].
$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of $C$ are given by

$$
\mathbf{r}(0)	= \left\langle 0, 0\right\rangle, \qquad
\mathbf{r}(2)	= \left\langle 2, 4\right\rangle.
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the path's endpoints defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(2,4).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(2))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(2,4)-f(0,0) \\  & ={2}^{2}\cdot {4}^{3}-{0}^{2}\cdot {0}^{3} \\  & =4\cdot 64 \\  & =256.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice how much faster it is to evaluate a line integral when we can use the fundamental theorem." :tutorial/id #uuid "8ce39e74-c98d-54af-8d93-20f6b5bca39a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5829 :tutorial/title "A Concrete Example"} :step/id #uuid "15f14408-48b8-5f0f-8c55-d5009dc56e57" :step/math-academy-id 35721 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134824}} {:db/id 17592186134861 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135128 :tutorial/content "Here, we prove the fundamental theorem of line integrals in the two-dimensional case. The three-dimensional case is similar.

Let $C$ be a smooth curve $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and suppose that $f(x,y)$ is a differentiable function of two variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ We wish to show that

$$
\int_C \nabla f \cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

Using our usual formula for calculating line integrals, we can write the left-hand side as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}∇f\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the chain rule, the integrand above is simply the derivative of $f(\mathbf r(t))$ with respect to $t.$ Thus, we can write this integral as

$$
\int_a^b \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d t}(f(\mathbf r(t)))\,\textrm d t.
$$

Finally, by the fundamental theorem of calculus, this is equal to 

$$
f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

This concludes the proof in the case where $C$ is smooth. It's easy to show that the theorem also holds for piecewise smooth curves." :tutorial/id #uuid "0ef0926c-7a69-5fc8-91f0-7f40e3be9be9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5830 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Fundamental Theorem for Smooth Curves"} :step/id #uuid "48691aa9-a37a-52cd-a44c-e9ef2b10ea85" :step/math-academy-id 35722}] :activity/title "The Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186133996} {:db/id 17592186134760 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135084 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b].$ The fundamental theorem of calculus states that

given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ⟩ \\ r(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,2\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

$y$-axis.

For example, the function 

$$
f(x) = x^2,

below enclosed by the curves $y=\sqrt x$ and $y=x$ is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the line $y=1$. Find the volume of the resulting solid.

![](images/36/362a92640ed68dfd5fa85f0338d95233003e9f8a1b059a5dffa2cda243a1411b.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} x & =\sqrt x \\[3pt] x-\sqrt x & = 0 \\[3pt] \sqrt x \left(\sqrt x - 1\right) &= 0 \\[3pt] x& = 0, 1 \end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1$.

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](images/54/5456bed18c03e823c8e9388571b5671f5f476f5caa1085793314b57080b2b07c.png)

The vertical arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=\sqrt{x}$, and
- *leaves* though the outer curver $y=x$.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

![](images/e8/e8f0f999521058f3213e11bd3df67a95a6ea8604e6853d06923ffbba6cf9d17c.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, to determine the limits of integration, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{2} &= 2 - y^{2} \\
2y^{2} &= 2 \\
y^{2} &= 1 \\
y &= ± 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=-1$ to $y=1$.

Next, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](images/c3/c3c9217600a26e11614752b2ca2ac8b3aa6c12b0df9f3a8c13d2b32c5b338107.png)

The horizontal arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=y^2$, and
- *leaves* though the outer curve $x={2-y^2}$.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of outer and inner solids.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x={2-y^2}$.![](images/36/3696bac064f5157b5c4ab3aefe34128d2d126a0a6b586106eb1e439bc90e7df5.png)
The corresponding volume is given by
$V_{outer}|= π\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1}[(right) - (left)]^{2}dy; = π\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1}[(2 - y^{2}) - (-1)]^{2}dy; = π\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1}[3 - y^{2}]^{2}dy$.
- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=y^2$.![](images/f5/f59ee5966f0cb9572d00e7f7278a7462841aef6b18f4865924303ad65b50738c.png)
The corresponding volume is given by
$V_{inner}|= π\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1}[(right) - (left)]^{2}dy; = π\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1}[(y^{2}) - (-1)]^{2}dy; = π\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1}[y^{2} + 1]^{2}dy$.
- **Step III.** Find the difference.Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as
$V|= V_{outer} - V_{inner}; = π\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1}[3 - y^{2}]^{2}dx - π\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1}[y^{2} + 1]^{2}dy; = π\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1}([3 - y^{2}]^{2} - [y^{2} + 1]^{2})dy; = π\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1}(8 - 8y^{2})dy; = \left.π(8y - \frac{8y^{3}}{3})\right|_{-1}^{1}; = π[(8 - \frac{8}{3}) - (-8 + \frac{8}{3})]; = π(\frac{32}{3}); = \frac{32π}{3}$."} {:db/id 17592186097208 :question/id #uuid "28406948-7dcf-5419-8190-83dae84e731e" :question/math-academy-id "q-30079"} {:db/id 17592186097209 :question/id #uuid "89556ba4-a6e5-533a-b6c1-5971b5251496" :question/math-academy-id "q-30118" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186096730 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3c6aa618-4d2f-5ce2-9bb2-c6b528ec9b7b" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bff877dd-2549-5c21-9e2a-6532f961d06a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{63π}{2}" :db/id 17592186095184} {:answer/id #uuid "e0f4e718-9113-5e14-b3a1-0832603fb983" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "21π" :db/id 17592186095185} {:answer/id #uuid "01ca3682-a08d-5f29-b1dd-5cc052a3dd12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{21π}{2}" :db/id 17592186095186} {:answer/id #uuid "6bb7b310-6130-5147-9dc4-46a2a12b4e87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{63π}{4}" :db/id 17592186095187} {:answer/id #uuid "77ca701e-f1df-516f-9397-34fd75769c4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{7π}{3}" :db/id 17592186095188}] :answer-field/id #uuid "6a5fce8d-1e83-5220-b88b-1bc28cf4c002" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186095183}] :question/problem "![](images/c6/c62793a0dc7ff37a4d6b7cf157239f21e6b0cdef8c3d428916f074584462598b.png)

Suppose that this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the horizontal line $y=-1$, generating a solid of revolution. How can we write an integral expression that gives the volume of the solid?

![](images/18/1880138e4a20cb5a47ba89cb3177d5dc6e74f998d7fdd428cdded7af38cadd02.png)

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{4} &= x \\
x^{4} - x &= 0 \\
x(x^{3} - 1) &= 0 \\
x &= 0, 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1$.

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](images/49/49da0885bbf23e586b488e2b2a9bcaa0d923d3591833c9b8beb31a611c1d8b43.png)

The vertical arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=x^4$, and
- *leaves* though the outer curve $y=x$.

Now, we can express the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves, as follows:

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y=x$.![](images/35/352ff26bb5dce0a923c102c4528bd89555b49203c212fb73a42cf31cdf8b226e.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{outer} &= π\int_{0}^{1}[(upper) - (lower)]^{2}dx \\
&= π\int_{0}^{1}[(x) - (-1)]^{2}dx \\
&= π\int_{0}^{1}[x + 1]^{2}dx
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=x^4$.![](images/ee/ee0fa31b61acd4a1f2a9b6bb21dcd0e5eed3c529780fcb67096d40dccf90c20c.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{inner} &= π\int_{0}^{1}[(upper) - (lower)]^{2}dx \\
&= π\int_{0}^{1}[(x^{4}) - (-1)]^{2}dx \\
&= π\int_{0}^{1}[x^{4} + 1]^{2}dx
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.
Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as
$V|= V_{outer} - V_{inner}; = π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}[x + 1]^{2}dx - π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}[x^{4} + 1]^{2}dx; = π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}([x + 1]^{2} - [x^{4} + 1]^{2})dx$." :tutorial/id #uuid "8e33de60-9df4-540e-b19b-f12088b349e2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1064 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "626bee34-cf24-50f9-b6b3-1fcbce8fe1a3" :step/math-academy-id 2092 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097659}} {:db/id 17592186097609 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096729 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096531 :question/id #uuid "b6dd2970-3cdc-58fc-8f28-0bfdcd738d6f" :question/math-academy-id "e-593"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2e0268f-36a5-5f55-a0ae-9e0f34981dab" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097228} {:db/id 17592186097229}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Horizontal Line"} :step/id #uuid "52be5c09-e883-51da-a981-64e4b7986356" :step/math-academy-id 2093 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097610}} {:db/id 17592186097610 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097797 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose that the region enclosed by the curves

$$

$$

![](images/78/7876211e2781a079ac2444436e671e2d61c28ec09774c0acad65e96fb537927a.png)

First, since we are rotating about a vertical line, we need to solve the equations of our curves for $x$:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}y = \frac{x}{2} & ⟹x = 2y \\ y = \sqrt{x} & ⟹x = y^{2}\end{bmatrix}

$$
\begin{aligned}
2y &= y^{2} \\
y^{2} - 2y &= 0 \\
y(y - 2) &= 0 \\
y &= 0, 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y={2}$.

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](images/c3/c3fd84335240208fb158da9b67aaffa07cf490c67f8a77bf28947df998180b76.png)

The horizontal arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x={y^2}$, and
- *leaves* though the outer curve $x=2y$.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{outer} &= π\int_{0}^{2}[(right) - (left)]^{2}dy \\
&= π\int_{0}^{2}[(2y) - (-2)]^{2}dy \\
&= π\int_{0}^{2}[2y + 2]^{2}dy
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=y^2$.![](images/cc/cca4c498956a16cb374a8d0b3341a09e52844026593557710525d07be79a233a.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{inner} &= π\int_{0}^{2}[(right) - (left)]^{2}dy \\
&= π\int_{0}^{2}[(y^{2}) - (-2)]^{2}dy \\
&= π\int_{0}^{2}[y^{2} + 2]^{2}dy
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as
$V|= V_{outer} - V_{inner}; = π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}[2y + 2]^{2}dy - π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}[y^{2} + 2]^{2}dy; = π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}([2y + 2]^{2} - [y^{2} + 2]^{2})dy; = break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let  $u=3+{x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{u})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2(3+{x}^{2})}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the first of the improper integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(-\frac{1}{2(3+{x}^{2})})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{2(3+0)}-\frac{1}{2(3+{a}^{2})}) \\  & =-(\frac{1}{6}-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **odd** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186253507 :question/id #uuid "21a2ef07-2c09-57fc-ace5-9d591df7b8d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-118777"} {:db/id 17592186288000 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We start by calculating the first of these integrals:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u={x}^{3}$,  then $\text{d}u=3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}+C \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{({e}^{{x}^{3}})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{0}-{e}^{{a}^{3}}) \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186320878 :question/id #uuid "85d0c74e-4503-59dc-b9ab-8cb0d6da3ead" :question/math-academy-id "q-351595"} {:db/id 17592186320879 :question/id #uuid "682ba32d-487c-5b43-bd26-2c39780def01" :question/math-academy-id "q-351600"} {:db/id 17592186320880 :question/id #uuid "5cdd21e7-31ed-571d-8af2-2513392df808" :question/math-academy-id "q-351605" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186105924 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d083b53b-8c39-5785-a250-5649001e822b" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Area of an Unbounded Region"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14d3be81-fa17-5678-892f-649528299dbb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186319449}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "14d3be81-fa17-5678-892f-649528299dbb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186319449} :answer-field/id #uuid "efd6a557-0dd5-5de4-9841-579dcad1aa36" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186320665}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the total area $A$ of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y=\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}$ and the $x$-axis.
