{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Let's sketch a graph of the region.

![](images/2b/2b7b85dd8894c73275816a8ee08a8c8a41fb41a327d20ed7bedc489f7e2e55ff.png)

We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x
$$

We start by calculating the first of these integrals:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u={x}^{2}$, then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{u}{3}))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}))|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{{a}^{2}}{3})) \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}(0-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{12}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}+\frac{\pi }{12} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186332946 :question/id #uuid "55c54cd7-0604-5984-8b9b-055f20084d5d" :question/math-academy-id "q-5966" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186105924 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d083b53b-8c39-5785-a250-5649001e822b" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Area of an Unbounded Region"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4fbbcb6c-2e6a-5a12-9d2e-23b23de5892e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{5\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186330675} {:answer/id #uuid "6400598e-ce3c-555e-ba3f-3969e7f485d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186330838} {:answer/id #uuid "703491e6-04b7-509f-b24e-1423bfa7f4a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186330956} {:answer/id #uuid "c1d34bc7-ffea-5420-9a4b-671380a6ae98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{9}" :db/id 17592186331673} {:answer/id #uuid "cecf1f59-e403-5aa0-a3f9-39fb9dc1ad4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186331785}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "703491e6-04b7-509f-b24e-1423bfa7f4a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186330956} :answer-field/id #uuid "ebe4f3fe-a5f0-5d9d-abc1-a06051457234" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186332614}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "![](images/dd/dd286aa5384dae22d8fff4bb29799078547064926697d71b0b0ca8739641408f.png)

$$

are unbounded:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x
$$

If the integrand $f(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty, \infty),$ then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x
$$

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results. 

**Watch out!** If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent." :tutorial/id #uuid "b58359c2-9f54-5bd7-8005-df9313559853" :tutorial/math-academy-id 932 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e2a6a97c-d17d-5e17-9d7b-d0d1dbe224ca" :step/math-academy-id 618349 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106953}} {:db/id 17592186106953 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105922 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105608 :question/id #uuid "dbd8b706-9ace-5adb-9c8e-29b0d21bfa82" :question/math-academy-id "e-515"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4e93fd7f-070f-5359-aabb-cba5cc275015" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048115} {:db/id 17592186048618} {:db/id 17592186051015}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106377} {:db/id 17592186106493} {:db/id 17592186253501} {:db/id 17592186253504} {:db/id 17592186288010} {:db/id 17592186351298}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Convergent or Divergent Integrals With Unbounded Limits"} :step/id #uuid "61313614-0ee3-57e5-8e4b-da016cba1b7b" :step/math-academy-id 618350 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106954}} {:db/id 17592186106954 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107099 :tutorial/content "Computing the definite integral of a function over the entire real line requires us to break the integral into two parts and separately evaluate each one.

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x
$$

Evaluating two improper integrals can be quite time-consuming. However, we can shorten the process if we see that $f(x)$ is an even or odd function. 

- Recall that $f(x)$ is an even function if $f(-x) = f(x).$ Even functions are symmetrical about the $y$-axis. Therefore, if $f(x)$ is even, we have

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x,
$$

provided that the integrals are convergent. Moreover, if $f(x)$ is even and the above integrals are convergent, then

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = 2\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

- Recall that $f(x)$ is an odd function if $f(-x) = -f(x).$ Therefore, if $f(x)$ is odd, we have

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = -\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x,
$$

provided that the integrals are convergent. Moreover, if $f(x)$ is odd and the above integrals are convergent, then

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "04e63304-93d0-5edd-985c-6a732614917f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4359 :tutorial/title "Improper Integrals of Even and Odd Functions"} :step/id #uuid :knowledge-point/title "Computing Covariance"}] :question/problem "Calculate $\textrm{Cov}(x,y)$ for the following data sets:

$$
x = \big\{ 6, \: -2, \: 7, \: 1 \big\},\qquad
y = \big\{ 5, \: -1, \: 4, \: 0 \big\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The (population) covariance of the data sets $x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}$ and $y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}$ is given by 

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) =  \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y}),
$$

where $\overline{x} = \dfrac{1}{n} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ and $\overline{y} = \dfrac{1}{n} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n y_i$ are the means of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the means:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{x} & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (6+(-2)+7+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 12 \\  & =3 \\ \overset{―}{y} & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (5+(-1)+4+0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 8 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance of our data sets is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(6-3)(5-2)+(-2-3)(-1-2)+(7-3)(4-2)+(1-3)(0-2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(3)(3)+(-5)(-3)+(4)(2)+(-2)(-2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[9+15+8+4] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 36 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050862} {:db/id 17592186176333 :question/id #uuid "9b3a2205-203a-5056-a951-45e86cc0afea" :question/math-academy-id "q-134066"} {:db/id 17592186176334 :question/id #uuid "23e49585-c742-508f-914d-dc9b039def78" :question/math-academy-id "q-134076"} {:db/id 17592186268969 :question/id #uuid "1d0e8ef1-dbd3-5d5d-b9cb-f3092550c8dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-134155" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186175936 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a2ac0065-9315-547a-a9cf-c6a5abea1aed" :knowledge-point/title "Computing Covariance"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "311e284a-a84b-5e7f-b5a1-e35c8f0d5168" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186266576} {:answer/id #uuid "64ccf930-ce1a-5735-bf79-470826f036dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186267036} {:answer/id #uuid "76132fbf-5e71-5e70-90ec-a505fc2186fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186267185} {:answer/id #uuid "853262fc-b92a-5438-baec-a53e6c209102" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186267317} {:answer/id #uuid "a31cd77b-6b2c-52dc-a626-7500d351a1a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186267611}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "311e284a-a84b-5e7f-b5a1-e35c8f0d5168" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186266576} :answer-field/id #uuid "aca651ef-8c84-5b8a-8875-73fe007986c0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186268716}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the following data sets:

$$

3591} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186176655 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176950 :tutorial/content "Given two finite data sets of equal length, say,

$$
x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}, \qquad 
y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\},
$$

the **covariance** between $x$ and $y,$ denoted by $\textrm{Cov}(x,y),$ is a measure that evaluates the extent to which $x$ and $y$ change together.

- A positive covariance means that if $x$ increases, then $y$ is also likely to increase:

![](images/bb/bbfae3f0fb38bc8652cd26716e4b0b128cf1f2039350267034d97161d7f5dac4.png)

- A negative covariance means that if $x$ increases, then $y$ is likely to decrease:

![](images/fd/fd45053fdc39f070e3438c3b8c61fe01613201595cfe00bd4cc6c6e481bf73ab.png)

- A covariance of zero (or close to zero) indicates that there is no *linear* relationship between $x$ and $y.$

![](images/a5/a58fa4d40d77af23df86b5bd8eaca3119b93bc9ea97cc435eb4e53ba2777b071.png)

 

**Watch Out!** A covariance of zero does *not* mean that $x$ and $y$ are not related. It simply means the relationship between them is not linear. To illustrate, consider the image below.

![](images/a4/a4bdbf92e691174644dda9b9a84acb1b896c0436afb221501dc10b4635841539.png)

 

The (nonlinear) relationship shown above is $y=x^2.$ However, it can be shown that $\textrm{Cov}(x,y) = 0$ for this data set.

To calculate $\textrm{Cov}(x,y),$ we use the following formula: 

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) =  \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y}),
$$

where $\overline{x}$  and $\overline{y}$ denote the means of $x$ and $y$ respectively.

**Note**: This formula for the covariance assumes that $x$ and $y$ are drawn from a *population*. There is a slightly different formula for covariance when $x$ and $y$ are sample data. However, we won't worry about the difference for now." :tutorial/id #uuid "da03b3e7-b452-59b9-b81e-5dd75cea02a2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10301 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid $$

y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}

If we compare a single data set, say $x$, against itself using our formula for covariance, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,x) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & ={\sigma }^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186172054 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "72015667-33a9-53e2-a0c4-09d8ce916b54" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Vector Fields That Are Independent of Path"}] :question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) =  \left\langle ye^{xy},\, xe^{xy}\right\rangle$ and the points $A(1,1)$ and $B(2,2)$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\mathbf F$ is conservative.

II. $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = e^4-e,$ where $C_1$ is the path along the curve $y=\sqrt{2x},$ traversed from $A$ to $B.$

III. $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = e^4-e,$ where $C_2$ is the path along along the line segment $\overline{AB},$ traversed from $A$ to $B.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Notice that $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ with domain $D = \mathbb R^2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = (1+xy)e^{xy}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives exist and are continuous and equal everywhere on $\mathbb R^2,$ we conclude that $\mathbf F$ is conservative. Therefore, we know there exists a function $f$ such that $\nabla f = \mathbf F.$

- Statement II is true. Since $\mathbf F$ is conservative, there exists a function $f$ such that $\nabla f = \mathbf F.$ Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f = e^{xy}.
$$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(2,2)-f(1,1) \\  & ={e}^{2\cdot 2}-{e}^{1\cdot 1} \\  & ={e}^{4}-e.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since $\mathbf F$ is conservative and $C_2$ has the same initial and terminal points as $C_1,$ we have

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = \displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = e^{4}-e.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186172299 :question/id #uuid "41a70c70-f13c-564f-a1cc-c8837528e651" :question/math-academy-id "q-125636" :knowledge-point/_questions 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=⟨y,\,-x⟩$ and the points $O(0,0)$ and $A(1,1)$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=0,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$

- **II.** ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=0,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the parabola $y={x}^{2},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$

- **III.** ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is independent of path.

- **IV.** $F$ is conservative." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Parameterizing the line segment, we have

$$
{r}_{1}(t)=⟨t,\,t⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}⟨t,\,-t⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,1⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t-t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Parameterizing the line segment, we have

$$
{r}_{2}(t)=⟨t,\,{t}^{2}⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}⟨{t}^{2},\,-t⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,2t⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}-2{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ have the same initial and terminal points, yet

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r\ne {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$

we conclude that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is path-dependent.

- Statement IV is false. If a vector field is conservative then it is path-independent. Since $F$ is path-dependent, it is not conservative."} {:db/id 17592186172300 :question/id #uuid "77c64f72-bc4e-5149-99d1-c9f993fca3fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-125663"} {:db/id 17592186259847 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,x\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩$ and the points $O(0,0)$ and $A(\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4},\frac{\pi }{2})$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $F$ is conservative.
- **II.** ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=1,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$
- **III.** ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4},$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Notice that $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ with domain $D={R}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.
$$

Since the partial derivatives exist and are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative.

- Statement II is false. Since $F$ is conservative, there exists a function $f$ such that $∇f=F.$ Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4},\frac{\pi }{2})-f(0,0) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}\cdot 1-0 \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since $F$ is conservative and ${C}_{2}$ has the same initial and terminal points as ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186259853 :question/id #uuid "230c0014-f97a-5ec3-b394-cdb780e495b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-125738"} {:db/id 17592186259861 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=⟨{y}^{2},\,-x⟩$ and the points $O(0,0)$ and $A(4,2)$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{5}{6},$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$
- **II.** ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{16}{3},$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$
- **III.** ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is independent of path.
- **IV.** $F$ is conservative." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Parameterizing the line segment, we have

$$
{r}_{1}(t)=⟨4t,\,2t⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}⟨4{t}^{2},\,-4t⟩\cdot ⟨4,\,2⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}16{t}^{2}-8t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\,{\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{2}-t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{[\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =8[\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}-0] \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Parameterizing the curve, we have

$$
{r}_{2}(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t⟩,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}⟨{t}^{2},\,-{t}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2t,\,1⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{{2}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{2}^{3}}{3})-0 \\  & =8-\frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ have the same initial and terminal points, yet

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r\ne {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$

we conclude that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is path-dependent.

- Statement IV is false. If a vector field is conservative then it is path-independent. Since $F$ is path-dependent, it is not conservative."} {:db/id 17592186415272 :question/id #uuid "0027cfb5-d932-549f-8cc6-973642895e8d" :question/math-academy-id "q-125743" :knowledge-point/_questions $$

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a))
$$

 

where $C$ is a piecewise-smooth curve $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and $f$ is differentiable function such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ 

This theorem tells us that the line integral of a conservative vector field $\mathbf{F} = \nabla f$ is determined by the values of $f$ at the endpoints $A$ and $B$ of $C$ only. The integral does *not* depend on the path between $A$ and $B.$ 

In particular, if $\mathbf F$ is conservative, then we say that $\displaystyle\int_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r$ is **path-independent.**" :tutorial/id #uuid Notice that $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ with domain $D={R}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2y.
$$

Since the partial derivatives exist and are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative. Therefore, we know there exists a function $f$ such that $∇f=F.$

Reconstructing $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f=x{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}.
$$

$$

Assume that $K>0.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **area** of a square **decreases** at a rate **inversely proportional** to **its side length**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *area $A$ of a square* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate *inversely proportional its side length*. In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{k}{s}
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.$

The area of a square is given by 

$$
A={s}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({s}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2s\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k}{s} \\ 2s\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k}{s} \\ \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k}{2{s}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2}>0
$$

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{K}{{s}^{2}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186373841 :question/id #uuid "20695e23-caba-5b56-9712-3007924a9859" :question/math-academy-id "q-143136"} {:db/id 17592186373848 :question/id #uuid *The **volume** of a cube **increases** at a rate that's **inversely proportional** to the **length of its edge**.* 

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cube* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *increases* at a rate that's *inversely proportional to the length of its edge.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{k}{s},
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cube is given by

$$
V={s}^{3}.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({s}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{s}^{2}\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{s} \\ 3{s}^{2}\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{s} \\ \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{3{s}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{3}>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=\frac{K}{{s}^{3}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186373806 :question/id #uuid "e52629c2-fde8-54a2-9c6a-177590506e80" :question/math-academy-id "q-143126"} {:db/id 17592186373813 :question/id #uuid constructing a differential equation to model a particular phenomenon, we sometimes combine several pieces of information to create the correct model.

Consider the following situation:

*The common cold virus spreads through a particular country. The rate at which the number of infected people increases is **proportional** to the **square of the time** $t$ (in days) since the outbreak started. 
Additionally, $100$ infected people **recover from the virus each day**.*

We want to find a differential equation that models $P(t),$ the number of infected people. We note the following:

- The statement describes the *rate* at which the *number of infected people* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d P}{\textrm d t}.
$$

- The rate at which the number of infected people increases is **proportional** to the **square of the time** $t.$ Therefore, if $I(t)$ represents the rate at which infections increase, then

$$
I(t) = kt^2,
$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.

- Additionally, $100$ infected people **recover from the virus each day**. Therefore, if $D(t)$ represents the rate at which infections decrease, then

$$
D(t) = 100.
$$

Therefore, the differential equation that describes this phenomenon is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t} & ={{k{t}^{2}-100}_{⏟}}_{I(t)-D(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Although we introduced the functions $I(t)$ and $D(t)$ here, we can usually write down the appropriate differential equation straight away. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a7ad3b5-e4de-56c0-8fc9-8a9b2c976094" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6270 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "37206e3d-9800-567e-82f6-eed74a977f1f" - The (smallest) distance between the point $(x,y)$ and the $x$-axis equals $|y|.$

- Similarly, the (smallest) distance between the point $(x,y)$ and the $y$-axis equals $|x|.$

- The slope of the line that passes through $(x,y)$ and the origin equals $\dfrac{y}{x}.$

value of the function $f(x,y) = 3x^2 - y^2$ given that $3x^2 + 2y^2\leq 16.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $\nabla f = \mathbf 0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨6x,-2y⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has the solution $(x,y)=\left(0,  0 \right).$ This point belongs to our region.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)= 3x^2 + 2y^2  = 16.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y), \qquad g(x,y)=16
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨6x,-2y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨6x,4y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}6x &=6\lambda x \\ -2y &=4\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(1-\lambda ) &=0 \\ y(2\lambda +1) &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)  =16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,y=\pm 2\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(0, \pm 2\sqrt 2 \right).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)  =16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,x=\pm \frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(\pm \dfrac{4\sqrt 3}{3}, 0 \right).$

- Note that assuming $\lambda = 1$ from the first equation leads to $y=0,$ which we already have a solution for, and $\lambda = -\dfrac12$ from the second equation leads to $x=0,$ which we also have a solution for. So, we have found all the candidates on the boundary.

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
\left( 0,0 \right), \qquad  \left( 0, \pm 2\sqrt 2 \right), \qquad \left(\pm \dfrac{4\sqrt 3}{3}, 0\right).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $\left( 0,0 \right)$ | $\left( 0, \pm 2\sqrt 2 \right)$ | $\left( \pm \dfrac{4\sqrt 3}{3}, 0 \right)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $-8$ | $16$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $\left(0, \pm 2\sqrt 2  \right),$ and its minimum value is $-8.$"} {:db/id 17592186048162} {:db/id 17592186199017 :question/id #uuid Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=16
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4x,-6y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨8x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=25
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-16y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,10y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2x &=2\lambda x \\ -16y &=10\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2x(1-\lambda ) &=0 \\ -2y(8+5\lambda ) &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=25$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2} & =25\,⇒\,y=\pm \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(0,\pm \sqrt{5}).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=25$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =25\,⇒\,x=\pm 5,\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(\pm 5,0).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm \sqrt{5}),\,(5,0),\,(0,0).
$$

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,\pm \sqrt{5})$ | $(\pm 5,0)$ | $(0,0)$ |

We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2x+1,2y+1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has the solution $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$ This point belongs to our region.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global maximum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=3
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x+1,2y+1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =1$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 1,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+1 &=2\lambda x \\ 2y+1 &=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{1}{2(\lambda -1)} \\ y &=\frac{1}{2(\lambda -1)}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,x=y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ in the condition $g(x,y)=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =3 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =3 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =3 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ x & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}),\,(-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}),\,(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2})$ | $(-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2})$ | $(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $3-\sqrt{6}$ | $3+\sqrt{6}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}),$ and its maximum value is $3+\sqrt{6}.$"} {:db/id 17592186389360 :question/id #uuid | $(x,y)$ | $(0,1)$ | $(\frac{\pm \sqrt{37}}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ |

Optimization Problems in Context"}] :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the maximum value of the sum of cosines of the angle measures of a triangle, given that all three angles are acute." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the measures of the angles. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = \cos{x}+\cos{y}+\cos{z},
$$

subject to the constraint

$$
x+y+z=\pi.
$$

Since the angles are acute, we also have the constraints $0 \lt x,y,z \lt \dfrac\pi 2.$ 

Let $g(x,y,z) = x+y+z.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y,z), \qquad g(x,y,z) = \pi
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,-\operatorname{sin}⁡z⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x &=\lambda \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡y &=\lambda \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡z &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sine function is one-to-one on the interval $\left( 0, \dfrac \pi 2\right),$ we can conclude that $x = y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y =x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =\pi  \\ x+x+x & =\pi  \\ 3x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

It's easy to show that this point is indeed the maximum and not the minimum. To do that, we can compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{12}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}) \\  & ≈1.47 \\  & <f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198945 :question/id #uuid "5440dc48-4c46-5737-826b-cf98fbacdffa" :question/math-academy-id "q-37701"} {:db/id 17592186199018 :question/id #uuid :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186362066}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "A rectangular box without a lid has a surface area of $48{\text{ cm}}^{2}.$ Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum possible volume of the box." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,y$, and $z$ be the box's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
2xz+2yz+xy=48.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=2xz+2yz+xy.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=48
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2z+y,2z+x,2x+2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}yz &=\lambda (2z+y) \\ xz &=\lambda (2z+x) \\ xy &=\lambda (2x+2y)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}xyz &=\lambda x(2z+y) \\ xyz &=\lambda y(2z+x) \\ xyz &=\lambda z(2x+2y)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $xyz=0,$ which contradicts the constraints. Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2z+y) & =y(2z+x) \\ 2xz+xy & =2yz+xy \\ xz & =yz\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z\ne 0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $x=y=2z.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2xz+2yz+xy & =48 \\ 4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =48 \\ 12{z}^{2} & =48 \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(4,4,2),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(4,4,2)=4\cdot 4\cdot 2=32\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2,5.5) & =2\cdot 2\cdot 5.5 \\  & =22 \\  & <f(4,4,2).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281547 :question/id #uuid "b8c68071-089c-5bff-bc03-ba61a8eab03b" :question/math-academy-id "q-162788" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198367 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "849449fb-bb08-54a3-b8ea-9f33ddd7a3e5" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Optimization Problems in Context"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18f121e3-ccfa-57b8-b6ef-a2e2cd0f3b57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186278810} {:answer/id #uuid "65b8a4fe-1d29-5ee2-ad9f-6c0583668e1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186279516} {:answer/id #uuid "76c3a733-f198-5a7c-a7fb-0c39f1adc2a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "13" :db/id 17592186279650} {:answer/id #uuid "8bf6ea47-eaeb-5270-89ec-aea8d1830cbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186279837} {:answer/id #uuid "944923f9-e97d-5493-8850-5c83f2a0ed3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "29" :db/id 17592186279911}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "65b8a4fe-1d29-5ee2-ad9f-6c0583668e1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186279516} :answer-field/id #uuid "797a794d-3c44-5cfd-9959-01ae83cb5934" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186281055}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the minimum possible sum of three positive numbers whose product is $27.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the three numbers. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=x+y+z,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=27.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=27
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}1 &=\lambda yz \\ 1 &=\lambda xz \\ 1 &=\lambda xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $1=0.$ Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}yz & =xz \\ yz-xz & =0 \\ (y-x)z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z>0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =27 \\ x(x)(x) & =27 \\ {x}^{3} & =27 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(3,3,3),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(3,3,3)=3+3+3=9.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(9,3,1) & =9+3+1 \\  & =13 \\  & >f(3,3,3).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362342 :question/id #uuid "1ec51af1-dbfa-5fa9-8f74-3c330eb163be" :question/math-academy-id "q-99163" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1609399a-f596-5865-ab9c-6aadc92d23db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "54\,\text{in}" :db/id 17592186360926} {:answer/id #uuid "3a4ae6f5-4806-5c92-95fb-a3ec3dd390a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "42\,\text{in}" :db/id 17592186361102} {:answer/id #uuid "838bc3f9-5547-5aae-9ce5-c937af91a9a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "60\,\text{in}" :db/id 17592186361421} {:answer/id #uuid "83aec126-3e7b-519c-90b5-432b36990afa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "72\,\text{in}" :db/id 17592186361422} {:answer/id #uuid "8c4af1fe-8cbf-5c53-aeb4-2b02ab93e510" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "48\,\text{in}" :db/id 17592186361456}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361421} :answer-field/id #uuid "e828baa6-f3ec-5068-b0c9-1c1c3f9d8a66" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362188}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A rectangular parallelepiped has a volume of $125\,{\text{in}}^{3}.$ Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, determine the minimum sum of the lengths of its edges." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the rectangular parallelepiped's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=4x+4y+4z,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=125.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=125
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨4,4,4⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4 &=\lambda yz \\ 4 &=\lambda xz \\ 4 &=\lambda xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x &=\lambda xyz \\ 4y &=\lambda xyz \\ 4z &=\lambda xyz\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =125 \\ x(x)(x) & =125 \\ {x}^{3} & =125 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(5,5,5),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(5,5,5)=4(5)+4(5)+4(5)=60\,\text{in}.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(25,5,1) & =4(25)+4(5)+4(1) \\  & =121 \\  & >f(5,5,5).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364648 :question/id #uuid "9021d181-6a6e-589c-8096-c7ad92921266" :question/math-academy-id "q-99230" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f027768c-f196-5e3f-adf4-7554b2177b3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "243\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364650} {:answer/id #uuid "f96459e6-4979-5896-b4e6-40cb50e3fdd2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "162\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364651} {:answer/id #uuid "5fe9f1a7-0904-5a92-b9f4-1e7ca2a2d4bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "128\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364652} {:answer/id #uuid "dc20d337-eb61-592e-aeed-865846e45bfb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "369\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364653} {:answer/id #uuid "42cfec62-7180-5eb9-8dbb-e33d7fe7ecf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "192\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364654}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364654} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ae58a56-6faf-52c9-9561-c87d35603ea0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364649}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A rectangular metal tank without a lid should hold $256\,{\text{ft}}^{3}$ of liquid. Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the tank's minimum possible surface area." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the tank's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy+2xz+2yz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=256.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=256
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨y+2z,x+2z,2x+2y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+2z &=\lambda yz \\ x+2z &=\lambda xz \\ 2x+2y &=\lambda xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x(y+2z) &=\lambda xyz \\ y(x+2z) &=\lambda xyz \\ z(2x+2y) &=\lambda xyz\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x(y+2z) & =y(x+2z) \\ xy+2xz & =xy+2yz \\ 2xz & =2yz \\ 2z(x-y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z>0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $x=y=2z.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =256 \\ (2z)(2z)z & =256 \\ 4{z}^{3} & =256 \\ {z}^{3} & =64 \\ z & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(8,8,4),$ and the minimum value is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(8,8,4)=8(8)+2(8)(4)+2(8)(4)=192\,{\text{ft}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(16,16,1) & =(16)(16)+2(16)(1)+2(16)(1) \\  & =320 \\  & >f(8,8,4).\end{aligned}

We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=108.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=108
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}yz &=2\lambda x \\ xz &=2\lambda y \\ xy &=2\lambda z\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}xyz &=2\lambda {x}^{2} \\ xyz &=2\lambda {y}^{2} \\ xyz &=2\lambda {z}^{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =108 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2} & =36 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(6,6,6),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(6,6,6)=6\cdot 6\cdot 6=216.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10,2,2) & =10\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =40 \\  & <f(6,6,6).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186446809 :question/id #uuid "1eb20554-7ec2-5620-86b4-093c81339236" :question/math-academy-id "q-99235" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198367 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "849449fb-bb08-54a3-b8ea-9f33ddd7a3e5" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Optimization Problems in Context"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2994103a-4373-5061-96dc-5e3036bdaad6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186446749} {:answer/id #uuid "8f6c4308-b2fa-5fef-b8c1-c5199b6fd2aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186446774} {:answer/id #uuid "a4b6bde5-927c-502e-9679-dbf365afa213" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{2}" :db/id 17592186446777} {:answer/id #uuid "b8f2b83f-9511-5453-b261-063e160979bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186446783} {:answer/id #uuid "bab5edc3-664a-5cc1-98e9-141f93a0f45d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186446785}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "2994103a-4373-5061-96dc-5e3036bdaad6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186446749} :answer-field/id #uuid "3dba08d8-907e-5202-bcd7-a010c639be80" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186446802}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, determine the maximum sum of the square roots of three positive numbers given that the sum of their squares is $27.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be three positive numbers. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z},
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=27.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=27
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}},\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}},\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} &=2\lambda x \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} &=2\lambda y \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}} &=2\lambda z\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Equivalently, we have

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{-3/2} &=4\lambda \\ {y}^{-3/2} &=4\lambda \\ {z}^{-3/2} &=4\lambda\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =27 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =27 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =27 \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(3,3,3),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(3,3,3)=\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3}=3\sqrt{3}.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5,1,1) & =\sqrt{5}+1+1 \\  & =2+\sqrt{5} \\  & <f(3,3,3).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186446810 :question/id #uuid "302ed073-7778-5ce1-8530-7759debd7de4" :question/math-academy-id "q-99203" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198367 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "849449fb-bb08-54a3-b8ea-9f33ddd7a3e5" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Optimization Problems in Context"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "11ccbc00-9325-556b-a2d6-4c11af9d456e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3+\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186446747} {:answer/id #uuid "5ea94620-3d10-5b50-b37f-bb7f9b5dfd37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1+\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186446760} {:answer/id #uuid "633619bf-d174-511b-822e-3e895a240fe7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186446761} {:answer/id #uuid "cdf3e77a-01de-506d-9a3b-29ed6a80b5d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186446789} {:answer/id #uuid "fe28be55-c646-5b66-9d92-47cfae8c06d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186446798}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "fe28be55-c646-5b66-9d92-47cfae8c06d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186446798} :answer-field/id #uuid "6cb2db16-47e5-539e-a0cd-d00a57818d78" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186446805}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, determine the maximum value of the sum of the sines of angle measures of a triangle." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the measures of the angles of the triangle. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡z,
$$

subject to the constraint

$$
x+y+z=\pi .
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $0<x,y,z<\pi .$

Let $g(x,y,z)=x+y+z.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=\pi 
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\operatorname{cos}⁡z⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x &=\lambda \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡y &=\lambda \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡z &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the cosine function is one-to-one on the interval $(0,\pi ),$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =\pi  \\ x+x+x & =\pi  \\ 3x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =1+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =1+\sqrt{2} \\  & <f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186446812 :question/id #uuid "71aa525f-c293-54c2-9046-61ecb78eb1e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-162796" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198367 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "849449fb-bb08-54a3-b8ea-9f33ddd7a3e5" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Optimization Problems in Context"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c1a0328-21a2-5d4a-be72-a0e945edf28f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186446751} {:answer/id #uuid "4026557b-c261-56b2-bc95-94093b494f38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186446754} {:answer/id #uuid "502949fc-7dbe-5b07-85d8-6afa9e12632d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186446757} {:answer/id #uuid "79fcac3f-eebf-518e-b439-901998e02ca4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186446767} {:answer/id #uuid "ecd42a19-38cc-5465-a5d7-71dd32273277" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186446796}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "4026557b-c261-56b2-bc95-94093b494f38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186446754} :answer-field/id #uuid "d16c3309-85b6-5b20-bebc-f505a6812eb7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186446808}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the maximum value of the sum of the cosines of three non-negative angles whose sum is $\frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the measures of the angles. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡z,
$$

subject to the constraint

$$
x+y+z=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

We also have the constraints $0\le x,y,z\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=x+y+z.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=\frac{\pi }{2}
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,-\operatorname{sin}⁡z⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x &=\lambda \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡y &=\lambda \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡z &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sine function is one-to-one on the interval $[0,\frac{\pi }{2}],$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =\frac{\pi }{2} \\ x+x+x & =\frac{\pi }{2} \\ 3x & =\frac{\pi }{2} \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2},0,0) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =2 \\  & <f(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186446814 :question/id #uuid "7a65655b-2417-5001-b909-d38270394c2a" :question/math-academy-id "q-162794"} {:db/id 17592186446818 :question/id #uuid #uuid "fb947756-3471-59c8-b3c4-9b21a1a91557" :question/math-academy-id "e-12457" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186198405 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9bbc1e6a-c728-5c5a-84f8-06a92c30a023" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Extreme Values: Cases With No Inner Critical Points"}] :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y) = x^2 + y$ given that $2x^2 + 3y^2 \leq 1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $\nabla f = \mathbf 0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2x,1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)= 2x^2 + 3y^2  = 1.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y), \qquad g(x,y)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,6y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2x &=4\lambda x \\ 1 &=6\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(1-2\lambda ) &=0 \\ \lambda y &=\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)  = 1$ implies

$$

1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical points in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}1 &=2\lambda x \\ 1 &=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{1}{2\lambda } \\ y &=\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,x=y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
y=x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),\,(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ | $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $10+\sqrt{2}$ | $10-\sqrt{2}$ |

#uuid "b82b3836-2ed6-522e-8a6b-e9301766e38d" :step/math-academy-id 32293} {:db/id 17592186199326 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199484 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the minimum and maximum values of the function

$$
f(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2
$$

subject to constraint $g(x,y) = x^2+y^2 \leq 1.$ In other words, we wish to find the global extrema of $f(x,y)$ defined on the disc of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown below.

![](images/5a/5ac34145b3911b19eb3775a915e8f0462c78502be6d6292e7682265c86eafce7.png)

  

To find the extrema, we proceed as follows:

- First, we find the critical points of $f$ inside the domain $x^2+y^2 < 1.$

- Then, we find the extreme values of $f$ subject to the constraint $x^2+y^2=1$ using the method of Lagrange multipliers.

- Finally, we determine the maximum and minimum values by evaluating $f$ at the candidate points.

Recall that the critical points of a function $f(x,y)$ are the solutions to $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \mathbf 0^T.$ Now, since the derivative of $f$ is the transpose of its gradient $\nabla f,$ the critical points are also given by the solutions to $\nabla f = \mathbf 0.$

So, we can find the critical points by solving $\nabla f = \mathbf 0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨4x,8y⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has the solution $(x,y)=(0,0).$ Note that this point belongs to our domain.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)= x^2 + y^2  = 1.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4x,8y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}4x &=2\lambda x \\ 8y &=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(2-\lambda ) &=0 \\ y(4-\lambda ) &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,y=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(0,\pm 1 \right).$

- Assuming $\lambda =2$ in the first equation, the second equation of the system implies

$$
\begin{aligned}y(4-2)=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,x=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $\left(\pm 1, 0 \right).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\pm 1, 0), \qquad (0, \pm1), \qquad (0,0).
$$

Note that we add the critical point $(0,0)$ to the list of the candidates above.

Finally, we evaluate $f$ at these points: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(\pm 1,0)$ | $(0, \pm 1)$ | $(0, 0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $4$ | $0$ |

$$
f(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2
$$

subject to constraint $g(x,y) = x^2+y^2 \leq 1.$ In other words, we wish to find the global extrema of $f(x,y)$ defined on the disc of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown below.

![](images/5a/5ac34145b3911b19eb3775a915e8f0462c78502be6d6292e7682265c86eafce7.png)

  

To find the extrema, we proceed as follows:

- First, we find the critical points of $f$ inside the domain $x^2+y^2 < 1.$

- Then, we find the extreme values of $f$ subject to the constraint $x^2+y^2=1$ using the method of Lagrange multipliers.

- Finally, we determine the maximum and minimum values by evaluating $f$ at the candidate points.

Recall that the critical points of a function $f(x,y)$ are the solutions to $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \mathbf 0^T.$ Now, since the derivative of $f$ is the transpose of its gradient $\nabla f,$ the critical points are also given by the solutions to $\nabla f = \mathbf 0.$

So, we can find the critical points by solving $\nabla f = \mathbf 0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨4x,8y⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has the solution $(x,y)=(0,0).$ Note that this point belongs to our domain.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)= x^2 + y^2  = 1.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4x,8y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}4x &=2\lambda x \\ 8y &=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(2-\lambda ) &=0 \\ y(4-\lambda ) &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,y=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(0,\pm 1 \right).$

- Assuming $\lambda =2$ in the first equation, the second equation of the system implies

$$
\begin{aligned}y(4-2)=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,x=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $\left(\pm 1, 0 \right).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\pm 1, 0), \qquad (0, \pm1), \qquad (0,0).
$$

Note that we add the critical point $(0,0)$ to the list of the candidates above.

Finally, we evaluate $f$ at these points: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(\pm 1,0)$ | $(0, \pm 1)$ | $(0, 0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $4$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum of $0$ at the point $(0, 0)$ and a maximum of $4$ at the points $(0, \pm 1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7cc22f9f-d1be-570d-acd7-d3f2e0af7a51"
